title: Charities cutting services due to financial pressures

By Rani Fletcher

By Monty Jacka

Topic:Community Organisations

The Tasmanian government has defended the level of funding given to community organisations across the state. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

Nearly half of Tasmanian community service organisations say they've had to cut some of their services due to a shortage of resources and additional financial pressures, according to the Tasmanian Council of Social Service (TasCOSS).

TasCOSS has warned that organisations could be forced to cut staff, turn people away and reduce their operating hours if nothing changes.

It's calling on the Tasmanian government to review funding agreements to enable community services to keep up with business costs.

Nearly half of Tasmania's community support organisations said they've had to cut services due to financial pressures, according to new data from the Tasmanian Council of Social Service (TasCOSS).

The 2026 Tasmanian Community Services Pulse Check surveyed more than 100 organisations across the state.

Sixty per cent said they had to turn people away in the past year and more than 80 per cent said they had experienced greater demand for their services despite their resources not increasing.

Community services are one of the largest industries in the state, employing roughly 28,000 people, TasCOSS says. (ABC News)

The Tasmanian Council of Social Service (TasCOSS) said, without change, organisations could be forced to cut staff, turn away community, and reduce operating hours.

The industry wants better indexation to help organisations keep up with business costs, and greater funding to match wage increases.

Up to 94 per cent of respondents said they experienced rising costs, and 58 per cent said funding has decreased in the last year.

TasCOSS chief executive officer Paula Wriedt said the community service industry was "in crisis".

Paula Wriedt says underfunding community services could later impact the health system, justice system, and other parts of government. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

She said state government funding hadn't kept up with service costs.

A Senate committee looking at cost of living issues has heard one charity estimates it is 10.5 million meals short of demand each year, while rising rents mean many are forced to choose between overcrowding or living rough.

"There's only so long that that can keep going until there are flow-on effects to our health system, to our justice system, to other parts of government that we may not anticipate," she said.

According to TasCOSS, community services are one of the largest industries in the state, employing roughly 28,000 people.

Ms Wriedt said there needed to be an equitable system of indexation.

"Three per cent doesn't even match some of the wage increases that have either come in already or are anticipated to come in in the future," she said.

Jordan River Service runs two Neighbourhood Houses in Gagebrook and Bridgewater, and offers a range of services from material support to social connection.

Proceeds from the Gagebrook Neighbourhood House cafe go directly back into local support programs. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

In the last year, chief executive Mel Best said the service had to cut its men's shed and fruit and vegetable box programs in order to stay afloat financially.

It also reduced its opening days to four days a week.

"This community in particular often loses services. We see transport services, public transport decreasing," she said.

Mel Best says Jordan River Service has had to make cuts to its offerings. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

Program coordinator Kylie Truswell said having to tell people that services were unavailable was tough.

"It's not a nice feeling; you don't want to turn anyone away or refuse to be able to provide food," she said.

"We have a lot of people come in, and they'll come in looking for food relief, free items.

Kylie Truswell says some in the community cannot afford to pay $6.50 for a meal. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

A spokesperson said the Tasmanian government "understand that costs are rising, which is exactly why the latest state budget invested more than $650 million into community organisations across Tasmania".

"This includes $4.8 million for TasCOSS, $55 million for Neighbourhood Houses, $7.1 million for food security providers and much more.

"There is a near $600 million investment into housing and homelessness services to put a roof over Tasmanians' heads when they need it most, and $235.4 million is available for electricity concessions."

The spokesperson said the government was "working with the sector to progress longer-term funding agreements, and we are committed to reviewing the level of indexation to provide certainty, in 2027-28".

Eric Abetz's first budget for Tasmania is coming — and community organisations fear they'll bear the brunt of funding cuts to "repair" the budget.

The Labor Opposition has called on the government to provide a sustainable funding model for community services.

"Every dollar the government fails to invest early will turn up later, and at far greater cost. In child safety, hospitals, homelessness services, police stations and the justice system," community services shadow minister Jess Greene said.

The Greens and Franklin Independent MP Peter George have also criticised the government.
